props.title: Long Pants

sections.content: **Long Pants** (1927) stands as a brilliant example of Harry Langdon's unique comedic style, markedly different from contemporaries like Chaplin and Keaton. Langdon plays a sheltered man-child experiencing his first pair of long pants, symbolizing an awkward transition into adulthood. The film's genius lies in its subversive take on coming-of-age stories, predating later works like **The Graduate** (1967) in exploring the uncomfortable space between adolescence and adulthood. Director Frank Capra, before his more famous works, demonstrates early mastery of mixing comedy with darker themes.

sections.content: Langdon's character represents a fascinating departure from silent comedy norms. While Chaplin played the clever underdog and Keaton the stoic hero, Langdon created a childlike innocent whose naivety often led to surprisingly dark situations. This approach influenced later character studies like **Being There** (1979) and **Forrest Gump** (1994), where seeming innocence confronts complex moral situations.

The film's treatment of sexuality and criminality was remarkably bold for 1927. When Langdon's character becomes infatuated with a female criminal, the film ventures into territory that even modern comedies might hesitate to explore. This complexity anticipates later works like **The Apartment** (1960) and **Harold and Maude** (1971) in mixing comedy with taboo subjects. SUBHEAD: The Capra Connection

sections.content: Frank Capra's early work with Langdon reveals a darker sensibility than his later feel-good classics like **It's a Wonderful Life** (1946). In **Long Pants**, Capra experiments with themes of innocence corrupted that would later appear in **Meet John Doe** (1941), though handled with much more optimism. The film's visual style, particularly in its dream sequences, shows remarkable sophistication for 1927.
